summary: For ages 8–9: interpret whole-number quotients so that one division expression (e.g. 56 ÷ 8 = 7) models TWO different actions — partitive/sharing ('56 shared among 8 → how many each?') and quotitive/grouping ('56 put into groups of 8 → how many groups?'). Both reach 7, but the story, the drawing, and what the 7 counts differ. Teach both structures explicitly by name, keep division tied to multiplication (8 × ? = 56), follow a concrete→pictorial→abstract progression, and introduce remainders informally through the same actions.
misconceptions: Believing division has only one meaning (sharing), so grouping/quotitive word problems are misread or mis-drawn.
Thinking division is commutative — that 56÷8 and 8÷56 are the same — by analogy with ×.
Sharing unequally or forgetting shares must be equal.
Believing the answer must always be smaller and being confused by remainders or by dividing a smaller by a larger number.
Divorcing ÷ from × and treating it as a standalone symbol rather than the inverse operation.

activities.title: Share-and-group the same pile
steps: Start with one pile of 56 counters.
First, SHARE: deal the counters one at a time, round-robin, into 8 plates until the pile is empty. Count how many landed on each plate (7).
Then, GROUP: from a fresh pile of 56, repeatedly scoop a group of 8 counters into a bag until the pile is empty. Count how many bags you made (7).
Write 56 ÷ 8 = 7 beside BOTH actions, then say aloud what the 7 means in each: '7 on each plate' versus '7 bags'.

Repeat both actions with 58 counters. When sharing, deal only full rounds (one to every plate) and stop when there are too few left to give all 8 plates one more. When grouping, stop when fewer than 8 counters remain. Notice the 2 leftover counters that cannot complete another round of equal shares or another group of 8. These are the remainder (58 ÷ 8 = 7 r2).
activities.insight: One division expression encodes two different questions. Doing both actions on the same quantity shows that 56 ÷ 8 lands on 7 either way, yet the 7 means 'number in each share' when sharing and 'number of groups' when grouping. Leftovers that cannot complete a share or a group are a remainder.

activities.title: Two panels, same expression
steps: Look at two side-by-side pictures: LEFT shows 8 plates of 7 counters; RIGHT shows 7 bags of 8 counters.
For the left picture, state what the answer counts ('how many on each plate'); for the right, state what it counts ('how many bags').
Write the single expression 56 ÷ 8 = 7 under both and answer: 'Both say 56 ÷ 8 = 7 — so what does the 7 count in each?'
Name each structure: left = sharing/partitive, right = grouping/quotitive.
activities.insight: The same expression and the same answer attach to two distinct meanings; naming each structure fixes the vocabulary of sharing versus grouping.

activities.title: Arrays and number lines: division as the inverse of multiplication
steps: Arrange the 56 counters as an ARRAY — 8 rows of 7 (or 7 rows of 8) — and write 8 × 7 = 56 alongside 56 ÷ 8 = 7 to see division as the inverse of multiplication.
Read the same array both ways: 8 rows of 7 counters, or 7 columns of 8 counters, each totalling 56.
On a NUMBER LINE, start at 56 and make equal backward hops of 8 until you reach 0; count the hops (7) — this is the number of groups of 8, the grouping/quotitive meaning.
Say how 8 × 7 = 56, 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and 56 ÷ 7 = 8 are all related through the same array.
activities.insight: An array makes division visible as the inverse of multiplication (8 × 7 = 56 ↔ 56 ÷ 8 = 7), and equal backward hops on a number line model the grouping meaning as repeated subtraction. Both keep division connected to multiplication rather than treated as an isolated symbol.

activities.title: Sort and match the stories
steps: Sort a set of word problems into two bins: 'sharing' and 'grouping'.
For 24 ÷ 6, choose which written story matches it as a GROUPING situation (making groups of 6) and explain your choice.
Explain why a story such as '6 shared among 24' (i.e. 6 ÷ 24) is NOT the same as 24 ÷ 6 — division is not commutative.
For each story you sort, say what each number stands for — the whole, the number of groups or the group size, and the answer.
activities.insight: Classifying and matching stories surfaces whether a learner holds only the sharing meaning and exposes the commutativity error (treating 24 ÷ 6 and 6 ÷ 24 as the same).

activities.title: The baker's choice
steps: Take the role of helping a baker split 56 rolls.
Decide and say aloud: do you want 8 boxes with the same number in each (sharing), or boxes that each hold 8 (grouping)?
Describe what changes between the two choices and what the answer 7 means in each.
Invent your own grouping story for 24 ÷ 6 and tell it to a partner.
activities.insight: Articulating the choice out loud prompts a learner to distinguish sharing from grouping and to say what each number represents, strengthening the language of the two structures.

checkQuestion: Here are two stories. Story A: '56 sweets shared equally among 8 children — how many each?' Story B: '56 sweets put into bags of 8 — how many bags?' Can they BOTH be written as 56 ÷ 8? Explain how each one is 56 ÷ 8.
checkAnswer: Yes — both are 56 ÷ 8. In Story A you know the number of groups (8 children) and find the size of each share (7 each); in Story B you know the group size (8 per bag) and find the number of groups (7 bags). Same division, two meanings.
